question.text:
The set $A$ and its boundary $\partial A$ are given by \[ A=\big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2: y < x+3\big\}, \qquad \partial A =\big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2: y = x+3\big\}. \]

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The point $P(-2,1)$ lies on the boundary of $A$
  2. The point $P(-2,1)$ belongs to $A$
  3. The point $Q(-2, 3)$ is an interior point of $A$
question.explanation:
Let $\delta >0.$ A neighborhood of a point $\mathbf x_0$ is the set of points whose distance from $\mathbf x_0$ is less than $\delta.$ \[ \{\mathbf x : |\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0| < \delta \} \]

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0$ is the open disc $|\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0| < \delta,$ as shown below.

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

  • A point $\mathbf x_0$ is an interior point of a set $S$ if $S$ contains some neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the interior of $S.$

  • A point $\mathbf x_0$ is a boundary point of a set $S$ if every neighborhood of $\mathbf x_0$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the boundary of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie below the line $y=x+3.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

Let's add the points $P(-2,1)$ and $Q(-2,3)$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

Let's examine the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. The coordinates of $P(-2, 1)$ satisfy $y = x+3.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $\partial A,$ the boundary of $A.$

  • Statement II is false. The coordinates of $P(-2, 1)$ do not satisfy the inequality $y < x+3.$ Hence, $P$ does not lie in the set $A.$

  • Statement III is false. Indeed, $Q$ is not an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point outside the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only.'

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
If we let $u = 4x,$ then \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{4} \,\textrm{d}u. \]

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

$x$ $\pi/12$ $\pi/8$
$u$ $\pi/3$ $\pi/2$

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int_{\pi/12}^{\pi/8} 3\csc^{2}(4x) \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} 3\csc^{2}(u) \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \csc^{2}(u) \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \left( -\cot(u) \right) \, \Big|_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \left( -\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \left( 0 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}} \end{align*}

question.text: Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda$ of the matrix $ A= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
First, we find the matrix $\, A-\lambda I \mathbin{:}$ ﻿﻿﻿\[ A - \lambda I = \begin{bmatrix} 4-\lambda & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{bmatrix} \]

The characteristic equation is $\det(A-\lambda I) = 0.$

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following:

\begin{align*} \det(A-\lambda I) &= 0 \\[5pt] \left| \begin{matrix} 4-\lambda & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{matrix}\right| &=0 \\[5pt] (4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)(6-\lambda) &=0 \\[5pt] (\lambda-4)(\lambda-3)(\lambda-6) &=0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=3,$ $\,\lambda_2=4,$ and $\lambda_3=6.$

Note: The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

question.text:
Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$, where

$\qquad$ $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }^{ A} \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} }^{ \mathbf{x}} &= \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} }^{ \mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can find the least-squares solution ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by $A^T\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} A^T \! A {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} &= A^T \mathbf{b} \end{align*}

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \! A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $(A^T \! A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

\begin{align*} {\hat{\mathbf{x}}} &= (A^T \! A)^{-1}A^T \mathbf{b} \\[5pt] &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \right)^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6& -3 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 3 \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac 4 3 \\1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -8 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \]

The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} . \]

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8 \end{bmatrix} ^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{3 \cdot (-8) - 9 \cdot (-2) }\begin{bmatrix} -8 & -9 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{3} & \dfrac{3}{2} \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} & -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{3} & \dfrac{3}{2} \\ -\dfrac{1}{3} & -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
Using the cumulative distribution function table of the binomial random variable $X \sim B(6, 0.26)$ given below, compute $P(3 \lt X \leq 5).$

$ \quad x \quad $ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$ $4$ $5$ $6$
$ P(X\leq x) $$\,0.1642\,$ $\,0.5104\,$ $\,0.8144\,$ $\,0.9569\,$ $\,0.9944\,$ $\,0.9997\,$ $\,1.0000\,$
question.explanation:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

\[ F(x) = P(X \leq x). \]

So, we have

\[ \begin{align*} F(5) &= P(X \leq 5) \\[3pt] &= P(X \in \{ 0,1,2,3,4,5 \}) \\[3pt] &= P(X \in \{ 0,1,2,3 \}) + P(X \in \{ 4,5 \}) \\[3pt] &= P(X \leq 3) + P(3 \lt X \leq 5) \\[3pt] &= F(3) + P(3 \lt X \leq 5). \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ \begin{align*} P(3 \lt X \leq 5) &= F(5) - F(3) \\[3pt] &= 0.9997 - 0.9569 \\[3pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0.0428}. \end{align*} \]

question.text:
Which of the following determinants are equal to $0?$

\[ |A| = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 4 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -2 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{array}\right|, \qquad |B| = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 0 & -2 & 9\\ 0 & 2 & \sqrt{3}\\ 0 & 1 & -8 \end{array} \right|,\qquad |C| = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} 0 & 2 & -4\\ 1 & \sqrt 5 & -2\sqrt 5\\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right| \]
question.explanation:
Let's examine each of the given determinants in turn.

  • The matrix $A$ is a diagonal matrix, hence \[ |A| = 4 \cdot (-2) \cdot 3 = -24 \neq 0. \]

  • The matrix $B$ has a zero column: \[ B=\begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}0} & -2 & 9\\ {\color{blue}0} & 2 & \sqrt{3}\\ {\color{blue}0} & 1 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \] As a result, $|B| = 0.$

  • The matrix $C$ has proportional columns: \[ C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-4} \\ 1 & {\color{blue}\sqrt 5} & {\color{blue}-2\sqrt 5} \\ 0 & {\color{blue}-1} & {\color{blue}2} \end{bmatrix} \] As a result, $|C| = 0.$

Therefore, only $|B|$ and $|C|$ are equal to $0.$
